title: Harvest and Visitor
premise: Odile Delacroix, a nonbinary property surveyor raised in foster care, is sent to appraise the abandoned Marchand house in rural Louisiana and finds their childhood imaginary friend, a figure called Wren, waiting on the porch exactly as they left him thirty years ago. The house appraises back—it measures the worth of everyone who enters, and it has been holding Odile's debt since 1974, when six-year-old Odile traded another child's life for their own survival. As Odile digs into the disappearance of a boy named Etienne, they uncover that the house's previous owners all paid its price with other people's futures, and that Wren is not an imaginary friend but the house's collector. To end it, Odile must return what was taken—offering the house something of equal value—and discovers that the only currency it will accept is the found family they've finally built, forcing them to choose between invisibility and being truly known.
about_author: Vesper Sterling is the pen name of a former insurance adjuster from the Gulf Coast who spent years documenting houses no one would insure twice. They write horror about paperwork, property lines, and the debts families pretend aren't inherited.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Arriving at the rotting Marchand house with a clipboard and professional skepticism, Odile begins the survey and notices small wrongnesses: rooms that measure differently on the second pass, a porch swing still warm. The beat is controlled unease—the rational mind cataloguing evidence it refuses to interpret.

chapters.title: Wren, Unchanged
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. On the second morning, Wren sits on the porch—a lanky figure in 1970s clothes, exactly as Odile imagined him at age six. He greets them by a name no one has used in decades. The emotional beat is vertigo: the past arriving intact, demanding to be acknowledged.

chapters.title: Comparable Properties
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, intercut with case files. Researching the house's history, Odile finds every owner vanished or ruined after selling, and a 1974 news clipping about a missing boy, Etienne Fontenot. The beat is dread deepening into purpose: this isn't haunting, it's bookkeeping.

chapters.title: What the House Measures
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The house begins appraising Odile—whispering figures, showing them their own life priced out: every foster home, every guarded year, every kindness declined as too expensive. Wren explains gently that nothing here is free. The beat is exposure; Odile's armor of self-sufficiency starts cracking.

chapters.title: The Summer of '74
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between adult Odile and fragmented memories. We learn six-year-old Odile, hiding during a violent night, was offered a bargain by the house's then-keeper: someone else taken instead. Etienne's name surfaces in Odile's own handwriting in an old notebook. The beat is guilt surfacing like a body in water.

chapters.title: Found People
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile calls the two people who've become family—Renata, a retired archivist, and Dez, a young coworker who idolizes them—and confesses everything. Instead of recoiling, they drive out to help. The beat is warmth against dread: being known for the first time, right before it might cost everything.

chapters.title: Terms of Sale
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, humanized. Wren reveals he was once a child taken by the house, remade into its collector, and that he has waited fifty years not to collect but to warn. The house wants a new keeper, and Odile is the only candidate whose debt makes them eligible. The beat is tragic tenderness—the monster as fellow victim.

chapters.title: Closing Costs
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Renata and Dez begin researching how to break the house's contract while the house turns hostile: doors rearranging, the appraisal figures climbing, Wren fading as his warning completes. The beat is rising panic—the deadline is the anniversary, three days away.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, climax. On the anniversary, Odile offers themselves as payment, but the house rejects a life given freely—it only accepts what is stolen. So Odile steals instead: they take the house's ledger, its memory of every debt, and burn it with Etienne's name read aloud first. Wren chooses to stay inside as it collapses, finally free to stop collecting. The beat is sacrifice transmuted into theft-as-mercy.

chapters.title: Fair Market Value
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, epilogue. Months later, Odile files the final report listing the Marchand house as condemned, value zero, and drives home to Renata and Dez's apartment where dinner is waiting. A wren lands on the windowsill and stays a moment. The beat is quiet resolution: invisible no longer, and learning that being seen was the price worth paying.
